title: Three facts, one card
hook: One flashcard asks for three facts. What does marking it right tell you?

knows: reading short labels and comparing simple counts
doesNotKnow: that a card with several answers can be marked right while one of them was missed, so one fact per card shows exactly which fact you missed

misconception: A card that asks for three facts at once works as well as three separate cards.
objective: Split a compound prompt into separately checkable cues.

claims.text: Scenario, hook and prediction: One flashcard asks for three facts. What does marking it right tell you? Card: 'Capital, currency and language of Peru?' You answer two of three and mark it right. What did the card record? Options: That you know all three / A pass that hides a miss. Correct option: A pass that hides a miss. claims.text: Separate cues expose separate gaps. A correct answer to one cue does not establish knowledge of the other two.
claims.source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science 17(3),249–255, DOI10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x; publisher abstract retrieved 2026-10-13: https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/ . claims.text: Stage: one card asks “Capital, currency and language of Peru?”. The stipulated answers are Lima · peso · Spanish, two of three right, as the question says. “Mark as one card” records one mark, right. “Split into 3 cards” marks capital Lima right, currency peso wrong (it is sol) and language Spanish right. Reveal sentences: As one card, the record is a single “right”: the missed currency left no trace. As three cards, the currency card is marked wrong (peso, not sol).

claims.text: Peru's capital is Lima, its currency is the sol, and Spanish is an official language of Peru (Quechua and Aymara are also official), so the stage counts Lima, sol and Spanish right and peso wrong.
claims.source: CIA World Factbook, Peru, https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/peru/ (capital; languages; exchange rates: soles per US dollar). Not opened by the builder in this session; for the fact-checker. Added by demo-builder 2026-10-15 (r11 fix plan); unverified. | FC pass 52 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, W-1144/W2): VERIFIED. cia.gov is blocked from this host (proxy 403; WebFetch DNS failure), so I opened the World Factbook's Peru entry through the factbook/factbook.json mirror (raw.githubusercontent.com/factbook/factbook.json/master/south-america/pe.json, fetched 2026-10-16, sha256 ff9c33e0fd34…). It reads: Capital 'Lima'; Languages 'Spanish (official) 82.9%, Quechua (official) 13.6%, Aymara (official) 1.6% … (2017 est.)'; Exchange rates 'nuevo sol (PEN) per US dollar'. So Lima, Spanish (official) and Quechua and Aymara (also official) are confirmed, and the currency is the sol/nuevo sol (PEN), not a peso. The Factbook still uses the pre-2015 name 'nuevo sol'. Ley 30381 (El Peruano, 14 Dec 2015) renamed it 'Sol', but I saw that only in search results; the official pages (elperuano.pe, bcrp.gob.pe) are blocked here. The stage's 'sol' is right either way. Caveat: this was a mirror, not cia.gov. Suggest demo-builder add a source that names the 'Sol' (BCRP or Ley 30381).

recall.question: A card asks 'Who signed the treaty, where and when?' and you get it half right. What change shows which part you missed?
options: Add more detail to the same card
Answer the same card faster next time
Split it into three cards, one fact each
recall.why: With one target per cue, each miss points at one fact; a compound card hides which part failed.
